question: Where do endocrine glands release their hormones directly?
explanation: Think of endocrine glands as ductless delivery systems. They pour their chemical messengers straight into the blood so they can travel all over the body! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h1)

question: A hormone travels through the whole body, but why does it only affect certain cells?

options.A: Non-target cells actively destroy the hormone on contact
options.B: The blood only carries the hormone toward specific organs
options.C: Target cells are the only ones physically close to endocrine glands
options.D: Target cells possess specific receptors that bind to that hormone

explanation: Hormones are like keys floating around, but they only fit into matching locks (receptors) on their specific target cells. Neat, right? [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h1)

question: Where do water-soluble (peptide) hormone receptors usually sit?
explanation: Since water-soluble hormones can't slip through the oily cell membrane, they have to catch their receptors right on the outer surface of the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h2)

question: How do lipid-soluble (steroid) hormones usually work inside a cell?

options.A: By using second messengers on the outside of the cell membrane
options.B: By blocking enzyme actions directly in the extracellular fluid
options.C: By binding to internal receptors and altering gene expression
options.D: By destroying the cell membrane to release stored energy

explanation: Because they love fats, steroid hormones slide right through the cell membrane, head inside, and talk directly to the cell's DNA to make new proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which pancreatic hormone is primarily responsible for lowering blood glucose levels?
explanation: Insulin facilitates the movement of glucose out of the bloodstream and into body cells, effectively lowering circulating blood sugar levels. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h3)

question: Your patient has an overactive thyroid (high T3 and T4). What sign would you most expect to see?

options.A: High blood sugar and frequent urination
options.B: Severe weight gain and feeling cold
options.C: Rapid weight loss and feeling warm
options.D: Slow resting heart rate and constant sleepiness

explanation: High thyroid hormone levels put the body's engine on overdrive! Patients burn through calories super fast, so they tend to lose weight quickly and feel hot all the time. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the kidneys?

options.A: Stimulating the excretion of excess water in urine
options.B: Blocking the reabsorption of sodium ions
options.C: Promoting water reabsorption into the blood
options.D: Increasing the production of red blood cells

explanation: Think of ADH as your body's water-saver. When you're running low on fluids, ADH tells your kidneys to hold onto water and put it back into your bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h4)

question: When blood pressure drops too low, how does aldosterone help bring it back up?

options.A: By forcing the heart to beat slower and weaker
options.B: By causing blood vessels to instantly dilate wide
options.C: By stopping the release of antidiuretic hormone
options.D: By causing the kidneys to reabsorb sodium and water

explanation: Aldosterone holds onto salt (sodium) in the kidneys. Water naturally follows salt into the blood, increasing your fluid volume and raising your blood pressure! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which gland releases growth hormone into the bloodstream?
explanation: The anterior pituitary is the powerhouse that churns out growth hormone, helping children grow taller and developing tissues all through childhood. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why are growth hormone and thyroid hormones so critical during infancy and childhood?

options.A: They regulate daily blood sugar levels after meals
options.B: They maintain normal calcium balance in the bones
options.C: They control the immediate fight-or-flight stress reaction
options.D: They coordinate normal skeletal growth and brain maturation

explanation: These two hormones work hand in hand to make sure a child's bones grow properly and their nervous system develops the way it should. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary male sex hormone responsible for secondary sex characteristics?
explanation: Testosterone is made mainly by the testes. It drives male reproductive development, muscle building, and masculine physical traits. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main job of progesterone during the female reproductive cycle?

options.A: Triggering the initial release of an egg from the ovary
options.B: Preparing and maintaining the uterine lining for pregnancy
options.C: Stimulating the growth of breast milk ducts at birth
options.D: Lowering female body temperature during menstruation

explanation: Progesterone prepares the uterus to welcome a fertilized egg and keeps that lining comfy and stable so a healthy pregnancy can start. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h6)

question: Which hormones flood the body right away during a sudden 'fight-or-flight' moment?
explanation: When you get a sudden fright, your adrenal medulla instantly pumps out adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline to get your body ready to run or fight! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h7)

question: How does long-term release of cortisol help the body cope with extended stress?

options.A: By increasing available blood glucose and energy supplies
options.B: By lowering the heart rate and blood pressure to rest
options.C: By promoting rapid storage of extra body fat in muscles
options.D: By enhancing digestion and nutrient absorption in the gut

explanation: Cortisol breaks down stored fats and proteins to keep your blood sugar up, ensuring your body has plenty of energy to push through tough, stressful times. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h7)

question: What type of feedback loop does the body mostly use to keep hormone levels balanced?
explanation: Negative feedback is like a home thermostat. When hormone levels get too high, a signal tells the gland to slow down and stop making more until things are balanced again. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h8)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a positive feedback loop in the human body?

options.A: Parathyroid hormone halting when blood calcium levels normalize
options.B: Insulin stopping the release of glucose once blood sugar drops
options.C: Oxytocin release intensifying uterine contractions during childbirth
options.D: Thyroid hormone stopping pituitary TSH release when levels are high

explanation: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback amplifies a signal! During labor, oxytocin makes contractions stronger, which releases even *more* oxytocin until the baby is born. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T5#GNS211_U1_T5_h8)
